text:
Keys guard the links between your tables. But what guards what goes INTO them? Say a product gets saved at minus three dollars. That's not a sale... that's a mistake. Your app could catch that. But a database rarely has just one writer. The web app, the mobile app, a nightly import, someone typing queries by hand. Each one has to remember the rule. And it only takes one that forgets.

So put the rule in the schema. That's a constraint: a rule the database checks on every write, whoever's writing. Price has to be zero or more. Try minus three... and Postgres refuses, naming the rule you broke. The bad row never lands. The notebook's still the only product. That error isn't a failure. It's the mistake caught at the door, while it's still cheap to fix. And every column has a rule before you add a single one.

Its type. Say quantity is an integer, and someone sends the word many. Refused. It isn't too big, or too small... it just isn't a number. A type decides which values can exist at all. So pick it from what the value means. And for money, that choice matters more than you'd think.

Add ten cents and twenty cents as floats, then ask Postgres if that's thirty cents. False! A float is approximate, so you get point three, a long run of zeros, and a four. Numeric is exact, so there the answer's true. That's the honest type for a price. So the value's the right kind. But does it have to be there at all?
